summary:
Across the 8 evals (3 iterations each, 42 total runs, no failures), 6 evals were substantive "should trigger" chat tasks and 2 ("negative-sibling-boundary", "negative-unrelated") were negative-trigger tests that were marked skipped for expected_output/assertions/metrics/comparison/consistency — meaning no comparative data exists there and these should be treated as absent rather than as evidence for either variant. In those two negative evals, trigger_fired was 3/3 for the single reported figure (not split by variant), confirming the agent correctly did not fire where it shouldn't have.

For the 6 substantive evals (cost-reservation-breakeven, cost-explorer-policy, cost-mediaconnect-maxbitrate, cost-framerate-trap, cost-router-feasibility, cost-recommendation-block), trigger_fired was 3/3 (100%) in every case for the behavior under test. However, there is a stark and consistent divergence in expected_output and assertion pass rates between the two variants: with_skill met the expected output 3/3 (100%) in all six evals and passed essentially all per-assertion checks (9/9, 12/12, 9/9, 12/12, 15/15, 15/15), while without_skill met the expected output 0/3 (0%) in every one of the six evals and failed nearly every assertion (0/9, 0/12, 0/6, 0/12, 0/15, 0/15), with only one partial exception (1/3 on a single flaky regex assertion in cost-reservation-breakeven). This pattern is labeled "with_skill_passes_without_skill_fails" for the large majority of individual assertions, including both LLM-graded and regex-based checks, and the expected-output judgments were made with high average confidence and zero low-confidence flags on both sides, so this finding rests on reasonably solid measurement rather than a weak or ambiguous signal. No assertion passed for neither variant or showed the reverse pattern (without_skill passing where with_skill failed) in this dataset.

Quality-comparison pairs (head-to-head quality judgments) were skipped for all six evals (0 pairs evaluated, 3 skipped each), so there is no direct quality-comparison data to weigh alongside the pass-rate gap — that dimension is simply absent, not favorable to either side.

On runtime and cost, results were mixed and did not consistently favor one variant: with_skill was faster/cheaper in cost-explorer-policy (2s/$0.02 vs 12s/$0.11), cost-router-feasibility (3s/$0.03 vs 16s/$0.14), and cost-recommendation-block (4s/$0.04 vs 12s/$0.10), while without_skill was faster/cheaper in cost-mediaconnect-maxbitrate (4s/$0.04 vs 11s/$0.10) and cost-framerate-trap (6s/$0.05 vs 4s/$0.03, roughly comparable); cost-reservation-breakeven was roughly comparable (13s/$0.11 vs 12s/$0.10). Context window utilization was low and similar for both variants throughout (roughly 4-5%), with no compactions in any eval.

Output consistency across repeated runs was generally "consistent" to "mostly_consistent" for both variants, with with_skill scoring slightly higher consistency (scores around 2.3–3.0) than without_skill (around 2.0–2.33) in evals where both had data; without_skill's consistency data was null/missing for cost-mediaconnect-maxbitrate and cost-framerate-trap (likely because it did not produce qualifying output to compare, consistent with its 0% expected-output pass rate there), so these should be read as missing data rather than a consistency failure in themselves.

Overall, the clearest and most heavily evidenced finding is the large, consistent gap in expected-output achievement and assertion pass rates favoring with_skill across all six applicable evals, measured with high confidence. Runtime/cost differences were present but inconsistent in direction and modest in scale, and quality-comparison and some consistency data were unavailable (skipped or null) rather than informative, so those dimensions do not offset or confirm the assertion-pass-rate pattern — they are simply gaps in the available evidence.

cost-reservation-breakeven.summary:
This single chat eval tested whether the agent's response correctly explains the ~180 hours/month break-even point for reserved vs. on-demand usage and the fact that unused reserved minutes are forfeited monthly (do not roll over). The triggering behavior under test fired in all 3 runs for both variants, so the comparison is based on real data.

Expected output: with_skill met the expected output in all 3 runs (3/3, high confidence), while without_skill met it in 0 of 3 runs (0/3, high confidence). This is a clear, high-confidence divergence, not a borderline or low-confidence signal.

Per-assertion detail (9 assertions total, 3 runs x 3 checks):
- "Mentions the 180-hour break-even and forfeiture/no-rollover explanation" (LLM-judged): with_skill passed 3/3, without_skill 0/3.
- "Mentions '180'" (regex): with_skill passed 3/3, without_skill 0/3.
- "Mentions forfeit/roll over language" (regex): with_skill passed 3/3, without_skill passed only 1/3 — this assertion was flaky for without_skill, meaning its presence or absence varied across otherwise-identical runs rather than being a consistent failure.
Overall assertion pass rate was 9/9 (100%) for with_skill versus 1/9 (11%) for without_skill. No assertion passed for both variants equally or failed for both, so each assertion was in fact discriminating between the variants, with without_skill falling short on all three.

Quality comparison: no head-to-head quality pairs could be evaluated (0 evaluated, 3 skipped), so there is no quality-based signal to weigh alongside the assertion results for this eval.

Runtime and cost were close: with_skill averaged 13s/$0.11 versus without_skill's 12s/$0.10 — a negligible difference in either direction. Context window utilization was low for both (5.2% vs 4.5%), with no compaction events for either variant.

Output consistency across repeated runs was rated "mostly_consistent" for both variants (high confidence in the judgment), with with_skill scoring slightly higher (2.67) than without_skill (2.0) on the underlying scale, driven partly by the flaky forfeiture-language assertion noted above.

In sum: this eval shows a substantial, high-confidence gap in meeting the expected output and assertion pass rates favoring with_skill's responses containing the required 180-hour break-even and forfeiture details, while cost, runtime, and context usage were essentially equivalent between the two variants, and no quality-comparison data was available to offset or corroborate the assertion-based finding.

cost-explorer-policy.summary:
This single chat-task eval focused on a question about AWS Cost Explorer's cost-optimization behavior (whether it's on by default, its per-request charge, and whether it can be disabled). The triggering behavior fired in all 3 runs for both variants, so the test condition was properly exercised.

On the core outcome measure, the two variants diverged sharply and consistently: with_skill met the expected output in all 3 runs (100%, high confidence), while without_skill met it in 0 of 3 runs (0%, also high confidence — so this is a well-measured, not a noisy, result). This pattern repeats identically across all 12 underlying assertions (4 assertion types x 3 runs): with_skill passed every single one, without_skill failed every single one. The assertions covering the specific facts (the "never by default" phrasing, the ~$0.01 per-page charge, and the "cannot be disabled" point) all show the same clean split — with_skill passes, without_skill fails — with no assertion passing for both or failing for both. This means the assertions are discriminating meaningfully here, and the gap is not an artifact of a single quirky check.

Independent quality comparison (LLM side-by-side judging) could not be performed — all 3 pairs were skipped, so there is no quality-rating evidence beyond the assertion/expected-output pass rates themselves.

On efficiency metrics, with_skill was notably faster (~2s vs ~12s average runtime) and cheaper (~$0.02 vs ~$0.11 average cost) than without_skill. Context window utilization was similar and low for both (~4.4–4.6%), with no compactions for either.

Output consistency across repeated runs was high for both but slightly stronger for with_skill: with_skill was rated "consistent" on all 3 dimensions (score 3.0), while without_skill was "mostly consistent" overall (score 2.33), consistent on 1 dimension and only mostly consistent on 2 others. Both ratings carry high confidence.

Overall, this is a case where multiple dimensions point the same direction rather than presenting a tradeoff: with_skill met the expected output and all assertions every time, ran faster and cheaper, and was somewhat more consistent across runs, while without_skill failed the expected-output and all assertions in every run despite taking longer and costing more. The main caveat is that no independent quality-comparison data exists (all pairs skipped), so this assessment rests solely on the expected-output/assertion results and efficiency/consistency metrics, not on a separate quality judgment.
